title: been backtesting my AI trading strategy for 3 months and the results are not what i expected
author: scheemermemer
selftext:
so i've been building and refining an AI based strategy for about 3 months now. spent a lot of time on the backtesting side before even thinking about going live with real money.

the strategy performs really well on paper. like almost too well which is exactly what makes me nervous about it. every time i see results that look too clean i start wondering if i've just curve fitted it perfectly to historical data without it actually being a robust strategy.

went live with a small amount just to see how it holds up in real market conditions and the results are noticeably different from the backtest. not catastrophic but different enough to make me question a few assumptions i built the whole thing around.

curious if anyone else has gone through this and what actually helped you close the gap between backtest performance and live performance. is it mostly a data quality issue, slippage, or something more fundamental in how the model was trained?

comments.author: CryptographerBig7624
comments.body:
the gap you're seeing is probably less about data quality or slippage and more about the model seeing patterns in hindsight it cant actually use forward. backtests let your logic peek at stuff that wouldnt be clear until later in live conditions

what helped me: stop training one model and start running multiple narrow agents that each look at one dimension only, then compare their verdicts. when they all agree you probably have something real. when one says go and another says skip you've caught exactly the kind of setup that looks good in backtest but falls apart live

also shadow-track the trades you skip. if your model keeps blocking setups that wouldve worked it means youre being too conservative. if it keeps blocking stuff that wouldve failed then the conservatism is earned. most people only measure what they took

comments.author: Fynca
comments.body:
If live results are meaningfully worse, I’d first suspect the backtest before the AI.

The big ones are data leakage, overfitting, unrealistic fills/slippage, and market regime differences. I’d run strict walk-forward testing on completely unseen periods and compare the model against a simple non-AI baseline.

If the AI only wins in-sample, the edge probably isn’t the model.

comments.author: Patient_Ant_5409
comments.body: The problem with training AI models for trading is that, generally speaking, the market is driven by news. When AI learns from historical data, it only sees candlesticks; it doesn't know which macroeconomic news events are moving the market. Personally, I use AI—I have over 2,000 AI models for various Forex pairs and some cryptocurrencies. However, I first apply a multi-timeframe pre-filter via code, then the AI ​​processes the data, and finally, it passes through a real-time news filter and economic calendar checks.

comments.author: yrobotus
comments.body: I ran into the exact same issue. Your models is probably getting data leakage from indicators providing data in the future.

replies.author: yrobotus
replies.body: By the way even the best model in the world won't be able to do well if the data it has access to doesn't give a full story.
